0-0: The Amateur Service exists for self-training, intercommunication and technical investigation by qualified people with a personal, non-commercial interest. Remember the three pillars: learn, talk, experiment - not profit or public utility work.
0-1: The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a specialised UN agency, coordinates global spectrum use and writes the international Radio Regulations that all member countries follow, preventing chaotic overlap of radio services worldwide.
0-2: MBIE is the government ministry that represents New Zealand at ITU conferences and coordinates the country's official position on international radio regulatory matters. NZART and IARU are amateur bodies, not the government voice.
0-3: The ITU splits the world into three regions for spectrum planning; New Zealand and the Asia-Pacific fall in Region 3, which affects which band allocations apply here. Remember: NZ is 'down under' in Region 3.
0-4: Amateur operation in New Zealand is governed by the New Zealand Radiocommunications Regulations, the statutory law under which licences and certificates are issued. Handbooks and ITU minutes are references, not the governing document.
0-5: Day-to-day administration of the Amateur Service is handled by MBIE's Radio Spectrum Management (RSM) group, the government body that manages spectrum licensing and enforcement in New Zealand.
0-6: Radio privacy rules forbid divulging the content or existence of any message you were not meant to receive. Overhearing is unavoidable, but repeating or acting on it is not permitted - treat it as if you never heard it.
0-7: Because radio operation can cause interference or breach rules at any hour, an authorised MBIE officer may inspect your Certificate of Competency at any time, not just during business hours.
0-8: The fundamental, top-level rules for the Amateur Service come from the ITU's International Radio Regulations; national regulations then implement these globally-agreed principles locally.
0-9: The Certificate of Competency qualifies you to transmit in the bands allocated to the Amateur Service. Receiving or repairing needs no certificate - it is the act of transmitting that requires qualification.
0-10: Your NZ certificate is valid throughout New Zealand and in any country that has agreed to recognise it (for example through CEPT), but it grants no automatic worldwide operating rights.
0-11: There is no restriction on the number of transmitters you may run simultaneously in your station, so you can operate several at once provided each stays within the rules.
0-12: You must keep your Certificate of Competency at the station so it can be produced for inspection. The other documents are useful references but are not legally required to be present.
0-13: An amateur station is defined by who runs it and where: a holder of a Certificate of Competency operating on the amateur bands. The purpose or the operator's profession does not define it.
0-14: Anyone holding an appropriate Certificate of Competency may operate the station in the owner's absence, because the qualification, not ownership, is what authorises operation.
0-15: Every station must have a reliable means of determining its operating frequency so the operator can stay within authorised bands, regardless of the mode being used. Knowing where you transmit is fundamental.
0-16: Unidentified transmissions are never permitted; all amateur transmissions must be identifiable by callsign. This lets stations be traced and holds operators accountable for what they send.
0-17: Amateur operation is licensed to the operator, not a fixed site, so you may operate portable elsewhere in New Zealand whenever you like without prior notice, as long as you follow the rules.
0-18: Mobile operation from a vehicle simply requires that you hold a current Certificate of Competency - the qualification travels with you. No extra callsign or notification is needed.
0-19: After passing the exam, only a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident may apply for the Certificate of Competency, tying the qualification to a genuine connection with New Zealand.
0-20: Current postal and email addresses are required so MBIE can contact the operator, for example about interference or regulatory matters. It is about reachability, not tracking station location.
0-21: The person actually at the controls is legally responsible for the station's proper operation. Whoever transmits carries the responsibility, regardless of who owns the equipment.
0-22: As operator, your core duty is ensuring the station operates properly and in accordance with the Radiocommunications Regulations. Compliance is your personal responsibility whenever you transmit.
0-23: A qualified operator must be present whenever the station transmits, because transmitting is the regulated activity. Receiving alone needs no qualified operator.
0-24: Keeping a logbook of stations worked is recommended good practice but not compulsory for amateurs. It is a useful record, yet the rules do not require it.
0-25: An unqualified family member cannot transmit alone because operating requires holding a Certificate of Competency. They may only operate under a qualified operator's direct supervision.
0-26: In New Zealand, NZART's Engineering and Licensing Group manages amateur repeater and beacon licence coordination, so repeater licence requests go there rather than directly to MBIE.
0-27: Amateur radio is non-commercial, so you may pass brief personal comments only if no fee or other consideration is requested or accepted. Business traffic for payment is forbidden.
0-28: There is no minimum age to hold a Certificate of Competency - anyone who passes the exam qualifies, so young people can become licensed amateurs.
0-29: The CEPT agreement lets a qualified NZ amateur operate in participating European countries without a separate licence, using their own callsign with a national prefix. Remember CEPT for European travel.
0-30: There is no upper age limit; the Certificate of Competency is held for life and never needs to be surrendered on account of age.
0-31: Peak envelope power is the average power measured at the crest (peak) of the modulation envelope - the highest average power in any one RF cycle at the modulation peak. It is the standard way to rate SSB output.
0-32: Maximum permitted power is set in the amateur General User Radio Licence (GURL), which lists limits per band rather than a single fixed figure, so always check the GURL for the band you are using.
0-33: At all times your output must not exceed the power limit listed in the GURL for that particular frequency band, since limits vary by band. The GURL is the authority on power.
0-34: You identify your station by transmitting your callsign, the unique official identifier that ties transmissions to you. Names or handles are not valid identification.
0-35: A valid NZ amateur callsign follows the ZL-prefix pattern: two letters, a single digit, then suffix letters, as in ZL2HF. The others do not fit the amateur callsign format.
0-36: Every NZ amateur callsign is recorded in the administration's (RSM's) database, which links each callsign to its holder. Callsigns are officially assigned, not invented by the operator.
0-37: New Zealand amateur callsigns generally begin with the prefix ZL (and related ZM/ZK blocks), the ITU-allocated identifier that marks a station as New Zealand's.
0-38: The digit in a NZ amateur callsign is a single figure from 1 to 4, historically indicating a geographic district within New Zealand.
0-39: A relinquished callsign is normally held back and only reissued after about one year, giving a reasonable interval before it returns to circulation.
0-40: The certificate authorises use of amateur transmitting apparatus; receivers and other equipment need no such authorisation because receiving is not a regulated act. It is transmitting that the certificate covers.
0-41: Certificates of Competency and callsigns are issued under the Regulations by MBIE-Approved Radio Examiners, who conduct exams and process applications on the ministry's behalf.
0-42: A replacement copy of your certificate can be downloaded and printed from the official database, either by you or by an Approved Radio Examiner - no re-examination is needed.
0-43: Permanent changes to your postal or email address must be advised to Radio Spectrum Management within one calendar month, keeping your contact details current for official communication.
0-44: The certificate contains the unique callsign or callsigns assigned to that operator. It identifies you and your callsign, but it is the GURL that actually authorises radiating radio waves.
0-45: A General Amateur Operator's Certificate of Competency is issued for life; once earned it does not expire or need renewal.
0-46: A General User Radio Licence (GURL) lets a whole class of transmitter be operated without each user holding an individual licence in their own name - amateurs operate under the amateur GURL.
0-47: An unqualified person may be permitted only to pass brief messages of a personal nature with no fee, and only under a qualified operator's supervision. The non-commercial, personal-only limit is key.
0-48: International third-party traffic may only be handled if the countries involved have expressly authorised such messages, since not all administrations permit passing messages for others across borders.
0-49: Third-party communications means messages sent to or on behalf of other people or organisations, rather than direct operator-to-operator conversation. Think: you relaying someone else's message.
0-50: SOS is the international Morse distress signal used only when a station is in grave and imminent danger and needs immediate assistance - the highest priority call for life-threatening emergencies.
0-51: If you hear distress traffic but cannot help, keep listening (maintain watch) until you are sure help is on its way, so you can act or relay if needed. Never simply ignore a distress call.
0-52: Secret codes obscuring meaning are forbidden because amateur transmissions must be open; the only exception is coded control signals used by licensees of remote beacon or repeater stations.
0-53: Using a secret cipher to hide meaning is expressly forbidden between amateur stations. Standard codes like ASCII or Baudot are fine because their meaning is public and decodable.
0-54: Harmful interference is defined as interference that obstructs or repeatedly interrupts a radiocommunication service operating under the regulations - the key is genuine disruption of a legitimate service.
0-55: If your station causes interference, you must immediately comply with any action MBIE requires to stop it. The obligation is immediate, not deferred until convenient or affordable.
0-56: Deliberately interfering with another transmission is never permitted, whatever the provocation. Even if another operator seems to be misbehaving, jamming is not an allowed response.
0-57: Newly qualified operators must first gain experience by operating for three months on bands below 5 MHz and above 25 MHz, logging fifty or more contacts, before wider privileges apply. It is a supervised familiarisation period.
0-58: Morse code (CW) may be used by any amateur operator; there is no longer a Morse test requirement, so it is open to all who wish to use it.
0-59: A New Zealand amateur may communicate with other amateur stations anywhere in the world, since amateur radio is inherently international - subject only to each country's own rules.
0-60: Amateurs are encouraged to train for and support disaster relief and emergency communications, reflecting the service's traditional role of providing communication when normal systems fail.
0-61: Your certificate permits operating an earth station in the amateur satellite service, letting you transmit to and through amateur satellites - a recognised part of amateur privileges.
0-62: A callsign like 'VK3XYZ stroke ZL' is an Australian (VK) amateur adding /ZL to show they are operating while visiting New Zealand - a normal, legal way to indicate a visitor's location.
0-63: HF (High Frequency) covers 3 MHz to 30 MHz. Remember the band names climb by decades: HF is 3-30 MHz, VHF 30-300 MHz, UHF 300-3000 MHz.
0-64: Bandplans allocate modes within bands by mutual agreement so operators do not interfere with one another - your operating does not disrupt others, and theirs does not disrupt you. They are voluntary courtesy, not law.
0-65: VHF (Very High Frequency) spans 30 MHz to 300 MHz, the decade above HF. This is where much local repeater and FM voice work takes place.
0-66: An operator must be able to verify that transmissions fall within an authorised frequency band, ensuring they never stray outside amateur allocations. Staying in-band is a fundamental competency.
0-67: An authorised MBIE official may order any amateur station closed down at any time, for example to stop interference. Neighbours or councils have no such power - only the regulator does.
0-68: Holding a certificate gives you no monopoly over any frequency or band; amateur allocations are shared, so you must cooperate and cannot claim exclusive use of a frequency.
0-69: A person in genuine distress may use any means available to attract attention and get help - normal procedures and frequency rules are set aside when life is at risk.
1-0: Amateur bands are shared, not divided into private channels, so operators are free to shift frequency within a band to dodge interference. Think 'agile' = able to nimbly move to a clearer spot.
1-1: New operators must log at least 50 contacts over their first 3 months on specified bands and keep that log for a year in case an official inspection is requested. It proves you are operating competently while learning.
1-2: The 80 metre band runs 3.50 to 3.90 MHz in New Zealand. Remember the metre name is roughly 300 divided by frequency in MHz, so ~3.7 MHz gives about 80 metres wavelength.
1-3: The NZ 40 metre band spans 7.00 to 7.30 MHz, wider than in some other countries. Anchor it as starting at 7.00 MHz and reaching 7.30 MHz.
1-4: The 20 metre band covers 14.00 to 14.35 MHz, a prime long-distance HF band. Note the upper edge is 14.35, not a round 14.5.
1-5: The 15 metre band runs 21.00 to 21.45 MHz. Its lower edge is a clean 21.00 MHz and it is 450 kHz wide.
1-6: The 10 metre band is unusually wide, 28.00 to 29.70 MHz, giving nearly 1.7 MHz of space including FM and satellite segments near the top.
1-7: The 2 metre VHF band is 144 to 148 MHz. A handy check: 300 divided by 146 MHz is about 2 metres wavelength.
1-8: The 70 cm band spans 430 to 440 MHz in New Zealand. Remember it is a 10 MHz-wide UHF band starting at 430 MHz.
1-9: Bandplans are voluntary agreements developed by NZART so amateurs share bands harmoniously, dividing them by mode and activity. They come from the amateur community itself, not from a government regulator.
1-10: The low-frequency 130 to 190 kHz band has a strict 5 watt e.i.r.p. limit because antennas there are tiny compared to wavelength and interference risk to other users is high.
1-11: Amateur satellites operate in segments of the 10 metre (28.0 to 29.7 MHz) and 2 metre (144 to 146 MHz) bands. These bands penetrate the ionosphere well enough to reach spacecraft.
1-12: The 2.4 GHz band (2400 to 2500 MHz) is shared with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, microwave ovens and other ISM devices, so amateurs must tolerate heavy congestion there.
1-13: The 7.1 to 7.3 MHz portion of 40 metres is shared with broadcasting and other services in some regions, so amateurs there have no exclusive claim.
1-14: The 146 to 148 MHz segment is shared with other communication services, so amateurs do not have exclusive access to all of the 2 metre band.
1-15: The 6 metre band, 51 to 54 MHz, is shared with other services in New Zealand, so amateurs must coexist and avoid causing interference there.
1-16: NZ bandplans are recommendations rather than law, but all operators are expected to follow them so everyone knows where to find each mode and activity.
1-17: On 21 to 21.45 MHz (15 metres) amateurs are the primary user, meaning they have first rights and are protected from interference by any secondary services.
1-18: As a secondary user, amateurs may operate only so long as they do not cause harmful interference to the primary service, and must accept interference from it. Secondary means you give way.
1-19: No one owns a frequency; both stations have equal rights, so the courteous newcomer checks whether the frequency is already in use and gives way if it is. First come, first served, with courtesy.
2-0: Silicon is a semiconductor: its conductivity sits between a metal and an insulator and can be controlled by adding impurities, which is why it forms the basis of diodes and transistors.
2-1: A material whose conductivity lies between an insulator and a conductor is a semiconductor. The 'semi' prefix literally means partway between.
2-2: An atom has a central nucleus of protons and neutrons, with light electrons orbiting around it. Only the electrons move around the outside and carry current.
2-3: Losing a negative electron leaves the atom with more protons than electrons, giving it a net positive charge, so it becomes a positive ion. Lose a negative, become positive.
2-4: Any current-carrying conductor is surrounded by a magnetic field, the basis of electromagnets, inductors and antennas. Moving charge always makes magnetism.
2-5: Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract, just like electric charges. North pushes north away; north pulls south in.
2-6: A loudspeaker uses a permanent magnet: a coil carrying the audio current is pushed and pulled against the fixed magnet to move the cone and make sound.
2-7: Copper conducts better than aluminium, carbon or silicon, which is why it is the standard material for wiring. Only silver beats it among common metals.
2-8: Resistance is the opposition to electron flow in a circuit, measured in ohms. More resistance means less current for a given voltage.
2-9: A conductor most readily allows current to flow because it has abundant free electrons, unlike an insulator, resistor or dielectric.
2-10: The plastic coating on wire is an insulator; it blocks current so the conductor is safe to touch and does not short against nearby wires.
2-11: A lithium ion battery is a source of electrical energy, converting stored chemical energy into voltage. Resistors, diodes and FETs only use or control energy, they do not supply it.
2-12: A lead acid battery is rechargeable, meaning its chemical reaction can be reversed by an external current, whereas a standard AA alkaline cell is designed for single use.
2-13: In a metal, rising temperature makes atoms vibrate more and impede electron flow, so resistance increases with temperature. Hotter metal, harder for electrons to pass.
2-14: N-type semiconductor is doped to have extra free electrons, so electrons are the majority current carriers. N for negative electrons.
2-15: P-type semiconductor is doped to have a shortage of electrons, creating positive vacancies called holes that carry the current. P for positive holes.
2-16: An insulator does not let electricity flow through it because its electrons are tightly bound and not free to move. That is what makes it useful for isolation and safety.
2-17: Glass, air, plastic and porcelain are all good insulators. The trick is spotting that lists containing copper, aluminium or carbon must be wrong since those conduct.
2-18: Gold, silver and aluminium are all good conductors. Watch out for lists that sneak in mica, wood or paper, which are insulators.
2-19: Current is the name for the flow of electrons through a circuit, measured in amperes. Voltage pushes it, resistance opposes it, but the flow itself is current.
3-0: Impedance, like resistance, is measured in ohms because it too is an opposition to current, but it applies to AC circuits. Ohms cover resistance, reactance and impedance alike.
3-1: The prefix kilo means one thousand, so one kilohm equals 1000 ohms. Kilo always multiplies by a thousand.
3-2: Kilo means one thousand, so one kilovolt is 1000 volts. Same thousand-fold rule applied to volts.
3-3: A quarter of an ampere is 0.25 A, and milli means thousandths, so 0.25 A equals 250 milliamperes. Multiply amps by 1000 to get milliamps.
3-4: The watt is the unit of power, the rate of using or delivering energy. In electricity, power equals voltage times current.
3-5: Milli means one thousandth, so two volts equals 2000 millivolts. To go from volts to millivolts you multiply by 1000.
3-6: The volt measures potential difference, the electrical pressure between two points that pushes current around a circuit. Think of it as the push behind the flow.
3-7: Impedance combines resistance (opposition that dissipates energy) with reactance (opposition from inductance and capacitance that stores energy). Both add together, vectorially, to give total AC opposition.
3-8: Milli means one thousandth, so one milliampere is one thousandth of an ampere. A small fraction of an amp.
3-9: Resistance is measured in ohms, named after Georg Ohm. Do not confuse the unit (ohm) with the component (resistor).
4-0: Ohm's Law gives voltage as current times resistance, E = I x R. More current or more resistance both raise the voltage drop across the component.
4-1: Using E = I x R with 0.01 A times 500 ohms gives 5 volts. Remember to convert 10 mA to 0.01 A before multiplying.
4-2: R = E / I gives 100 V divided by 0.0008 A, which equals 125,000 ohms, or 125 kilohms. Convert 0.8 mA to 0.0008 A first.
4-3: I = E / R is Ohm's Law, showing current equals voltage divided by resistance. It is the foundational relationship linking the three quantities.
4-4: E = I x R gives 4.4 A times 50 ohms, which equals 220 volts. Straight multiplication of current and resistance.
4-5: E = I x R gives 2 A times 16 ohms, which equals 32 volts. The applied voltage equals the drop across the resistor.
4-6: E = I x R gives 5 A times 50 ohms, which equals 250 volts. Larger current through the same resistance means a larger voltage.
4-7: E = I x R gives 0.2 A times 25 ohms, which equals 5 volts. Convert 200 mA to 0.2 A before multiplying.
4-8: By Ohm's Law current is proportional to voltage in a fixed resistance, so halving the current from 0.5 A to 0.25 A means halving the voltage from 6 V to 3 V.
4-9: Current equals voltage divided by resistance, I = E / R. Raising voltage increases current, while raising resistance reduces it.
4-10: By I = E / R the current is 12 divided by 8 amps. Voltage goes on top, resistance on the bottom.
4-11: I = E / R gives 50 V divided by 100 ohms, which is 0.5 A, or 500 milliamperes. Express the half-amp in milliamps to match the answer.
4-12: Resistance equals voltage divided by current, R = E / I. It is Ohm's Law rearranged to solve for the resistance.
4-13: R = E / I gives 10 V divided by 0.001 A, which equals 10,000 ohms, or 10 kilohms. Convert 1 mA to 0.001 A first.
4-14: R = E / I gives 3 V divided by 0.3 A, which equals 10 ohms. Convert 300 mA to 0.3 A before dividing.
4-15: R = E / I gives 12 V divided by 0.5 A, which equals 24 ohms. Dividing by a half doubles the number.
4-16: Greatest opposition means the largest resistance; 0.5 megohms is 500,000 ohms, far bigger than the others. Convert everything to ohms to compare fairly.
4-17: The ohm is the unit of electrical resistance, the opposition to current flow. Volts measure pressure and amperes measure flow, but ohms measure the opposition.
4-18: R = E / I gives 12 V divided by 0.15 A, which equals 80 ohms. Smaller current from the same voltage implies larger resistance.
4-19: I = E / R gives 12 V divided by 4800 ohms, which equals 0.0025 A, or 2.5 mA. A large resistance yields a tiny current.
5-0: Adding a parallel branch gives current another path, so overall opposition drops. The total is always below the smallest single resistor because every branch adds conductance. Remember: parallel resistance is always less than the least.
5-1: Each 1000 ohm resistor draws I=V/R=40/1000=40 mA, and parallel branch currents add, giving 80 mA total. Same voltage sits across both branches, so just sum the two currents.
5-2: In parallel the source current splits among branches, so by Kirchhoff's current law the total equals the sum of all branch currents. Think of a river dividing into channels that must carry all the flow.
5-3: A series resistor drops the surplus 6 V so only 3 V reaches the lamp. In series the same current flows and voltages add, so the resistor and lamp share the 9 V supply.
5-4: Parallel loads each draw their own current from the supply, so divide 5 A by 0.25 A per lamp to get 20. Total current is the limit, and branch currents simply add up.
5-5: In series the voltages add, so six 2 V bulbs need 6 x 2 = 12 V to each get their rated 2 V. Series shares the supply voltage across all components.
5-6: Series voltages add, so the number of bulbs is the supply voltage divided by each bulb's voltage: 240/12. Each bulb must receive its rated 12 V for the string to light normally.
5-7: Equal series resistors split the supply voltage equally, so each of three drops 90/3 = 30 V. In series the same current flows and voltage divides in proportion to resistance.
5-8: For two in parallel use product-over-sum: (75x50)/(75+50)=3750/125=30 ohms. The result is always below the smaller value, confirming 30 is sensible.
5-9: Every cell has internal resistance; large current through it causes an internal voltage drop, so terminal voltage falls below the open-circuit value. More current means more sag from this hidden resistance.
5-10: Product-over-sum: (6x30)/(6+30)=180/36=5 ohms. Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest branch, so being below 6 ohms is expected.
5-11: Series resistances simply add, so the total must exceed any single resistor. Each added resistor puts more opposition in the same current path, increasing the total.
5-12: Series resistances add directly, so 5 x 10 = 50 ohms. Identical resistors in series give a total of the value times the count.
5-13: Series resistors add: 10+270+3900+100 = 4280 ohms. Simply sum all values in a series string to get the total.
5-14: Series values add, so five 24 ohm resistors give 5 x 24 = 120 ohms. Look for the option whose sum equals the target value.
5-15: Convert to common units and add: 2.2 M + 0.1 M = 2.3 megohms (100 kilohm is 0.1 megohm). Series resistances add once units match.
5-16: Equal resistors in parallel give R divided by the number of them, so ten give R/10. Each identical branch adds conductance equally, dividing the total resistance.
5-17: Equal parallel resistors give value divided by count: 68/4 = 17 ohms. This shortcut works only when all resistors are identical.
5-18: Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest branch, and here the smallest is 10 ohms, so the total must be under 10 ohms. Extra branches only lower it further.
5-19: Three 47 ohm resistors in series add to 141 ohms, closest to 150. Series adds values while parallel would give a much smaller result, so series suits this target.
5-20: Two equal 120 ohm resistors in parallel halve the value to 60 ohms. Equal parallel pairs always give half of one resistor's value.
5-21: Parallel branches share the same voltage, so by I=V/R the branch carrying twice the current must have half the resistance. More current at equal voltage means lower resistance.
5-22: Parallel always gives less than series, and five equal 1 k resistors in parallel give 1000/5 = 200 ohms. Parallel divides the value, so it yields the smallest possible resistance.
5-23: Two 28 ohm resistors in parallel give 14 ohms, then adding a third 28 ohm in series gives 14+28 = 42 ohms. Combining parallel then series builds intermediate values.
5-24: Two 100 ohm resistors in parallel give 50 ohms, then adding the 10 ohm series resistor totals 60 ohms. Solve the parallel section first, then add the series part.
5-25: Series resistances add to 15 ohms, so I=V/R=15/15=1 ampere. In series, current is the supply voltage divided by the total resistance.
5-26: Three 12 ohm in parallel give 4 ohms, so I=V/R=8/4=2 amperes. Find the parallel total first, then apply Ohm's law.
5-27: The same 100 mA flows through each series resistor, so each drops V=IR=0.1x33=3.3 volts. In series, voltage across one resistor is its own resistance times the shared current.
5-28: Equal parallel resistors give value over count: 300/6 = 50 ohms. Dividing the resistor value by the number of parallel units reaches the required load.
5-29: Three 500 ohm in series total 1500 ohms; shorting the middle one removes its 500 ohms, leaving 1000 ohms. A short circuit bypasses a component, subtracting its resistance.
6-0: Power equals voltage times current: 300 V x 0.03 A = 9 watts. Convert milliamps to amps first, then multiply by volts to get watts.
6-1: Power is volts times amps: 12 V x 0.5 A = 6 watts. Always change 500 mA to 0.5 A before multiplying.
6-2: Each resistor safely handles 1 watt, so two together can dissipate 2 watts total. Power ratings add regardless of whether resistors are in series or parallel.
6-3: Each resistor is rated 5 watts, so two share a combined 10 watt capacity. Total power handling is the sum of the individual ratings.
6-4: Use P=I squared x R: (0.01)squared x 100000 = 0.0001 x 100000 = 10 watts. Squaring the current then multiplying by resistance gives the dissipation.
6-5: P=I squared x R: (0.5)squared x 1000 = 0.25 x 1000 = 250 watts. Remember to square the current before multiplying by resistance.
6-6: P=I squared x R: (0.25)squared x 20 = 0.0625 x 20 = 1.25 watts. Square the current first, then scale by resistance.
6-7: With voltage and resistance, use P=V squared / R: 200squared/2000 = 40000/2000 = 20 watts. This form avoids needing the current.
6-8: From P=I squared x R, rearrange to I=square root of (P/R)=square root of (500/20)=square root of 25=5 amps. Solve for current when power and resistance are known.
6-9: The watt is the SI unit of power, the rate of using energy. One watt equals one joule per second, or one volt times one amp.
6-10: Power is the product of voltage and current: P=V x I. This is the fundamental electrical power formula to memorise.
6-11: A watt equals a volt times an ampere, since P=V x I. Multiplying these two base electrical units yields power in watts.
6-12: P=V x I = 10 V x 0.01 A = 0.1 watt. Convert milliamps to amps before multiplying by the voltage.
6-13: Two 10 ohm in series total 20 ohms, so P=V squared/R=100/20=5 watts. Find total resistance first, then use the voltage-squared power formula.
6-14: Total power is 9 x 4 = 36 watts, and with P=V x I, current = 36/12 = 3 amperes. Sum the power, then divide by supply voltage to get the series current.
6-15: Each 18 ohm resistor across 12 V dissipates V squared/R = 144/18 = 8 watts, and three give 24 watts. In parallel each sees full voltage, so add their individual powers.
6-16: P=I squared x R: (0.02)squared x 10000 = 0.0004 x 10000 = 4 watts. Square the current in amps, then multiply by resistance in ohms.
6-17: Overheating means the resistor is dissipating more power than its rating, turning excess electrical energy into heat. Exceeding the wattage rating is what causes burning.
6-18: For a resistor, rms current gives P=I squared x R=100 x 100=10000 watts; frequency does not matter for a pure resistance. Using rms values makes AC power calculate like DC.
6-19: Power depends on voltage squared (P=V squared/R), so doubling voltage multiplies power by four. Any voltage change has a squared effect on dissipated power.
7-0: Alternating current periodically reverses its direction of flow, unlike DC which flows one way. The mains and radio signals alternate back and forth many times per second.
7-1: Period is the reciprocal of frequency: 1/100 = 0.01 second. More cycles per second means each cycle takes less time.
7-2: Hertz counts cycles per second, so 50 Hz means 50 complete cycles occur each second. Frequency describes how often the waveform repeats, not voltage or current.
7-3: Frequency is one divided by the period: 1/0.1 = 10 Hz. A longer time per cycle means a lower frequency.
7-4: A harmonic is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental, and 4 kHz is twice 2 kHz (the second harmonic). Transmitters must suppress harmonics to avoid interference on other bands.
7-5: One thousand cycles per second is one kilohertz (kHz). Hertz replaced the old 'cycles per second', with kilo meaning one thousand.
7-6: Mega means one million and kilo one thousand, so 1 MHz = 1000 kHz. Each step up the prefix ladder multiplies by one thousand.
7-7: Giga is one thousand times mega, so 1 GHz = 1000 MHz. Remember the ladder: hertz, kilo, mega, giga, each a factor of a thousand.
7-8: For a sine wave the rms value is 0.707 (1 over root 2) times the peak. Rms is the effective value that delivers the same heating power as an equivalent DC.
7-9: Rms equals 0.707 times peak, so 10 A peak gives 7.07 A rms. Multiply the peak by 0.707 to find the effective sine-wave value.
8-0: Capacitors in series combine like resistors in parallel, so the total is always less than the smallest one. Series stacks the dielectric gaps, reducing overall capacitance.
8-1: Series capacitors share the applied voltage, so each sees only part of it, letting the string withstand a higher total voltage. The trade-off is reduced total capacitance.
8-2: Capacitance is measured in farads, and practical values are usually microfarads. The unit in a component's rating tells you what type it is.
8-3: Capacitance increases as plate spacing decreases, so bringing the plates closer doubles it. Closer plates create a stronger field for the same charge, storing more.
8-4: The insulating material between capacitor plates is the dielectric. Its type and thickness set the capacitance and the voltage the capacitor can withstand.
8-5: Capacitors in parallel add, so three 15 pF give 45 pF. Parallel plates effectively increase total plate area, so capacitances sum.
8-6: The frequency-dependent opposition that capacitors and inductors present to AC is called reactance. Unlike resistance it stores and returns energy rather than dissipating it.
8-7: Capacitive reactance is inversely proportional to frequency, so it rises as frequency falls. At low frequencies a capacitor blocks AC; at high frequencies it passes it easily.
8-8: Inductive reactance is proportional to frequency, so it increases as frequency rises. An inductor passes low frequencies readily but chokes high frequencies.
8-9: Inductance increases with more turns; roughly it grows with the square of the turn count. More turns link more magnetic flux, raising inductance.
8-10: The henry is the unit of inductance. It measures how effectively a coil opposes changes in current by producing back-EMF.
8-11: Inductors in series add like resistors, so two 20 uH give 40 uH. Series windings combine their inductances directly.
8-12: Inductors in parallel combine like resistors, so two equal 20 uH give half, 10 uH. Parallel paths divide the total inductance.
8-13: A toroid is wound on a closed ring of magnetic material, which keeps the magnetic field contained within the core. This self-shielding reduces stray coupling to nearby circuits.
8-14: Transformer output follows the turns ratio: 230 x (10/100) = 23 volts. A step-down turns ratio reduces the secondary voltage proportionally.
8-15: At series resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, leaving only small resistance, so impedance is minimum and current maximum. Think series-resonance equals series-minimum.
8-16: At parallel resonance the branch currents cancel in the external circuit, so impedance is maximum and line current minimum. Parallel-resonance equals maximum impedance, the 'tank' circuit.
8-17: Inductive reactance is 2 x pi x f x L = 2 x 3.14 x 3.5e6 x 0.005, roughly 110000 ohms or 110 kiloohms. Reactance rises with both frequency and inductance.
8-18: Resonance occurs when inductive and capacitive reactances are equal and opposite, so the inductor must also be 500 ohms. Matching the reactances is the condition for resonance.
8-19: A high-Q circuit has low losses and a narrow bandwidth, making it highly selective at picking out one frequency. Higher Q means a sharper, more selective response.
9-0: The current source must be removed before touching the casualty, otherwise you become part of the circuit and get shocked too. Safety rule: switch off first, rescue second.
9-1: Killing the power and unplugging removes the live mains before you work, so no energy can reach you. Isolate the equipment first; capacitors can still hold charge, so treat everything as live until proven safe.
9-2: Good insulation stops high-voltage wires touching each other or the chassis, which would cause a short circuit and possible damage or fire. Insulation keeps current on its intended path.
9-3: An RCD compares the current flowing out in the phase with that returning in the neutral; any imbalance means current is leaking to earth (possibly through a person), so it trips fast to prevent electrocution.
9-4: Earthing the chassis holds it at the safe earth potential. If a live wire touches it, heavy fault current flows to earth and blows the fuse instead of leaving the chassis dangerously live to touch.
9-5: The earth conductor bonds the metal chassis to earth, so an internal fault to the chassis trips the fuse rather than making the case live. It protects you from a shock if you touch the equipment.
9-6: In the modern colour code the phase (live) wire is brown. Memory hook: Brown = Bringer of power.
9-7: The neutral wire is blue in the modern colour code. Memory hook: BLue = Neutral (both cool colours), while brown is live.
9-8: The earth (protective) conductor uses green-and-yellow striped insulation, chosen to be unmistakable. Memory hook: green = ground/grass, the safety earth.
9-9: An isolating transformer has no direct connection between its output and earth, so neither output lead is referenced to ground. This means touching one lead alone won't complete a circuit to earth, reducing shock risk.
10-0: The transistor is the fundamental semiconductor amplifier: a small base/gate signal controls a much larger current, giving gain. Diodes only conduct one way and cannot amplify.
10-1: A zener diode holds a nearly constant voltage across it when reverse-biased into breakdown, making it ideal as a voltage regulator or reference. Memory hook: Zener = Zteady voltage.
10-2: Germanium junctions conduct at a lower forward voltage (about 0.3V) than silicon (about 0.6-0.7V) because of germanium's smaller band gap. Lower drop makes germanium useful for low-level signal detection.
10-3: A bipolar junction transistor's three terminals are emitter, base and collector. The base controls current flowing from emitter to collector.
10-4: All bipolar transistors, PNP or NPN, use the same three terminal names: collector, emitter and base. Only the polarity of the junctions differs.
10-5: Producing a larger output from a smaller input signal is amplification, the defining function of an active device like a transistor. The extra energy comes from the power supply, not the input.
10-6: Silicon rectifier diodes dominate power supplies because silicon tolerates higher temperatures, voltages and currents cheaply and reliably. Germanium's low forward drop can't offset its poor thermal handling here.
10-7: Recovering the original information from a modulated carrier is demodulation (detection), and a diode does this by rectifying the signal. It reverses what modulation did at the transmitter.
10-8: Under forward bias the N region's free electrons are pushed across the junction into the P region, so electron flow is n to p. Conventional current, by convention, flows the opposite way (p to n).
10-9: Silicon is the classic semiconductor: its conductivity sits between conductors and insulators and can be controlled by doping. Copper is a conductor; sulphur is an insulator.
10-10: A varactor (varicap) diode's reverse-bias depletion layer acts like a capacitor whose value changes with the applied voltage, so it behaves as a voltage-controlled variable capacitor, useful for tuning.
10-11: Doping means adding tiny amounts of impurity atoms to pure silicon to create extra free electrons (N-type) or holes (P-type), giving the material its useful controllable conductivity.
10-12: A diode's two terminals are the anode (positive, current enters) and the cathode (negative, marked by a band). Current flows easily from anode to cathode only.
10-13: A bipolar transistor has three leads: emitter, base and collector. This matches its three-region NPN or PNP structure.
10-14: NPN (and PNP) describes the layer structure of a bipolar transistor. So an NPN audio device is a bipolar transistor; FETs use channel types instead.
10-15: Bipolar transistors come in two polarities, NPN and PNP, named for the order of their doped layers. The polarity sets the direction of supply voltage and currents.
10-16: Excess heat from too much current or voltage destroys a transistor's junctions. Good heatsinking and staying within ratings prevent thermal failure.
10-17: With zero base-emitter voltage (base at emitter potential) the junction can't turn on, so no collector current flows: the transistor is cut off. It needs roughly 0.6V forward bias to conduct.
10-18: Field-effect transistors come as N-channel and P-channel types, named for whether electrons or holes carry current through the channel. The gate voltage controls the channel.
10-19: Gate, drain and source are the terminal names of a field-effect transistor (FET), where the gate voltage controls current from source to drain. Bipolar transistors use base/emitter/collector instead.
11-0: On a bipolar transistor symbol the base is the flat bar that both other electrodes connect to. For NPN the emitter arrow points away from the base (Not Pointing iN).
11-1: The collector and emitter are the two angled leads; the emitter carries the arrow, so the plain angled lead is the collector. In NPN the emitter arrow points outward, away from the base.
11-2: The base is always the straight bar contacting the other two leads. A PNP is identified by the emitter arrow pointing inward toward the base (Points iN, Proudly).
11-3: The emitter is the lead bearing the arrowhead; in a PNP that arrow points inward toward the base. Identifying the arrow direction distinguishes PNP from NPN.
11-4: On a junction FET symbol the gate is the single lead entering the side of the channel bar. An N-channel JFET has the gate arrow pointing in toward the channel.
11-5: The drain and source are the two ends of the FET's channel bar; the arrow on the gate pointing inward marks it as N-channel. Drain and source are the current-carrying terminals.
11-6: On a MOSFET symbol the gate is the electrode separated from the channel by a gap, representing the insulating oxide layer. That insulated gate is what distinguishes a MOSFET from a JFET.
11-7: Two separate insulated gate electrodes on one channel identify a dual-gate MOSFET, commonly used in RF mixers and amplifiers where a second gate provides gain control or a second input.
11-8: In a valve symbol the grid is drawn as a dashed line between cathode and anode; a tetrode has two grids. The grid controls electron flow much like a transistor's base.
11-9: A tetrode has a control grid and a screen grid; the screen grid sits between control grid and anode to reduce inter-electrode capacitance and improve gain at high frequencies.
12-0: An ohmmeter passes a known small current through the component and reads the resulting voltage to display resistance in ohms. Always measure resistors with power off, out of circuit.
12-1: In the reverse position an SWR meter samples power travelling back from the antenna, i.e. reflected power. High reflected power means a poor match; ideally it should be near zero.
12-2: Current is measured with an ammeter, connected in series so all the supply current flows through it. Volts, watts and ohms are different quantities needing different meters.
12-3: The receiver runs on DC from its supply, so a DC ammeter in series measures the current drawn. An RF ammeter would only respond to radio-frequency currents, not the DC supply.
12-4: A real ammeter has a small but non-zero internal resistance, so in circuit it behaves as a low-value resistance in series. Keeping it low minimises the voltage it steals from the load.
12-5: An ammeter must be in series so the whole current passes through it; break one supply lead and insert the meter. Connecting it in parallel would short the supply through the meter.
12-6: An ammeter has near-zero resistance, so across a battery it acts as a short circuit; huge current flows and burns out the meter. Ammeters go in series, never straight across a source.
12-7: An ammeter needs very low internal resistance so inserting it in series barely disturbs the circuit current it is meant to measure. Ideally it would be zero ohms.
12-8: A voltmeter connects across (in parallel with) the circuit, so it must have very high resistance to draw negligible current and avoid loading down the voltage it reads. Ideally infinite.
12-9: For a sinewave, RMS equals peak divided by root-2 (peak x 0.707). So 14V peak x 0.707 is about 10V RMS. RMS is the effective heating value of the AC waveform.
13-0: Decibels for power are 10 x log10(ratio). A 10x power ratio is log10(10)=1, so 10 x 1 = 10 dB. Memory hook: every factor of 10 in power = 10 dB.
13-1: A 100x power ratio is 10 x log10(100) = 10 x 2 = 20 dB. Each tenfold power increase adds another 10 dB, so 100x is two steps = 20 dB.
13-2: Working backwards, 20 dB means log10(ratio)=2, so the power ratio is 10^2 = 100. Every 10 dB multiplies power by 10, so 20 dB is 10x10.
13-3: 10 dB corresponds to a power ratio of 10^(10/10) = 10^1 = 10. Ten dB always means ten times the power.
13-4: EIRP = transmitter power + antenna gain - feedline loss in dB. To stay at the 14 dBW limit: 14 = Tx + 7 - 1, so Tx = 8 dBW, which is about 6.25W. The antenna gain adds to your effective radiated power.
13-5: Attenuation in dB is 10 x log10(input/output). 10W in, 1W out is a 10x reduction = 10 dB. Attenuation is just negative gain.
13-6: Halving the power (10W to 5W) is 10 x log10(2) = 3 dB. Memory hook: 3 dB is always a factor of two in power, up or down.
13-7: Gains in dB simply add when stages are cascaded: 10 + 40 = 50 dB. Using dB turns multiplying ratios into simple addition.
13-8: Attenuation counts as negative gain, so add algebraically: 20 dB gain minus 10 dB loss = 10 dB net. dB values just sum along the chain.
13-9: Cascaded gains add in dB, so three 5 dB stages give 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 dB total. Adding dB replaces multiplying the individual power ratios.
14-0: A linear amplifier is an optional stage boosting the transceiver's output when more power is needed, while preserving the signal's waveform (linearity) so SSB and other modes aren't distorted.
14-1: The extra path bypassing the amplifier block is a switch that routes the signal around it, letting the operator take the linear amp out of circuit to run at the transceiver's lower barefoot power.
14-2: The low-pass filter sits in the main output path, so it must handle the station's full transmit power without overheating or breaking down. It suppresses harmonics above the operating frequency.
14-3: An SWR bridge monitors the standing-wave ratio on the feedline, revealing how well the antenna is matched. A high SWR warns of reflected power and a poor match needing correction.
14-4: The antenna switch selects between the real antenna and a dummy load, letting you tune up into the dummy load without radiating and interfering with others.
14-5: An antenna tuner (ATU) transforms the antenna system's impedance to match the transceiver's output (typically 50 ohms), presenting a good load so the transmitter delivers full power. It matches, not physically retunes the antenna.
14-6: A dummy load is a non-radiating resistor that absorbs the transmitter's power, letting you test and adjust the rig off-air without causing interference. It mimics an antenna's impedance without emitting.
14-7: Feedlines between station stages are coaxial cable, whose shield contains the RF and provides a controlled 50 ohm impedance while rejecting interference. Coax is the standard unbalanced feeder.
14-8: A tuner is only needed to correct an impedance mismatch. If the antenna's input impedance already equals the transceiver's output impedance, the match is perfect and no tuner is required.
14-9: The run to the antenna is normally 50 ohm coaxial cable, matching the standard station impedance and shielding the RF feed. Coax is the usual unbalanced feeder for HF antennas.
15-0: The RF amplifier is the first gain stage after the antenna, boosting the tiny incoming signal so later stages have enough level to work with. Think: RF amp lifts the weak signal early.
15-1: A mixer heterodynes the incoming signal with the local oscillator, producing sum and difference frequencies; the difference is the fixed intermediate frequency (IF). Mixing two frequencies creates a new, easier-to-process IF.
15-2: The local oscillator must run at a frequency offset from the signal so their difference equals the IF, so it matches neither the signal nor the IF. LO minus signal equals IF.
15-3: A mixer generates several products (sum, difference, and originals); the IF filter passes only the wanted intermediate frequency and rejects the rest. The filter cleans up the mixer's messy output.
15-4: IF stands for intermediate frequency, the fixed frequency to which every signal is converted so amplification and filtering can be optimised at one point. Intermediate = the middle step between RF and audio.
15-5: A product detector mixes the IF signal with a carrier oscillator to recover the original audio, translating the RF-domain signal down to hearable audio frequencies. It multiplies signal by carrier to get audio.
15-6: The AF (audio frequency) amplifier raises the weak recovered audio to a level able to drive a loudspeaker or headphones. AF amp simply makes the audio loud enough to hear.
15-7: BFO means beat frequency oscillator; it injects a tone that beats with the IF to produce an audible note for CW and to demodulate SSB. Remember: it creates a beat you can hear.
15-8: Because the IF is a single fixed frequency, several tuned stages can be cascaded there for high, stable gain, so most receiver gain lives in the IF amplifier. Fixed frequency allows the most gain.
15-9: As the first stage handling the weakest signal, the RF amplifier must add very little noise of its own, since any noise here is amplified through the whole chain. The front end sets the noise floor.
15-10: The mixer beats the signal against the local oscillator to shift it to the fixed IF, so its job is changing the signal frequency. Mixer = frequency changer.
15-11: DSP means digital signal processing, where the signal is handled numerically by software to filter, demodulate and reduce noise. DSP does the maths that hardware used to do.
15-12: FM carries information in frequency, not amplitude, so the limiter clips off any amplitude variations (like noise) before demodulation. Limit the amplitude, keep only the frequency changes.
15-13: A phase-locked loop tracks the incoming frequency and its control voltage follows the modulation, making it an effective FM demodulator. PLL locks on and its correction voltage is the audio.
15-14: In a communications receiver the AF amplifier boosts the recovered voice-band audio to drive a speaker; speech occupies roughly the audio range it handles. It amplifies the speech you hear.
15-15: Volume (audio gain) is controlled in the AF amplifier stage, since that is where the audio level is set before the speaker. Turn the volume, adjust the AF amp.
15-16: Selectivity, the ability to separate adjacent signals, is set by the narrow IF filter's bandwidth. The filter defines how selective the receiver is.
15-17: Narrowband FM communications channels need roughly a 10 kHz filter bandwidth to pass the signal while rejecting adjacent channels. Match the filter to the FM channel spacing.
15-18: In an SDR the digitised signal is demodulated numerically inside the DSP by software, not by analogue circuits. The DSP does the demodulation in maths.
15-19: An SDR's behaviour is defined by code running in the DSP, so software is loaded or changed there. Software-defined radio means the DSP holds the software.
16-0: Frequency stability is a receiver's ability to hold its tuning on the wanted signal without drifting, mainly depending on oscillator steadiness. Stable = stays put on the signal.
16-1: Sensitivity describes how weak a signal a receiver can still usefully detect. High sensitivity means it hears faint signals.
16-2: The weakest detectable signal is limited by the receiver's own internally generated noise, so the quieter receiver wins. Less internal noise means it hears fainter signals.
16-3: Sensitivity is specified as the signal-plus-noise to noise ratio, showing how far a weak signal rises above the receiver's noise. It quantifies signal against noise.
16-4: A more sensitive receiver produces more usable signal relative to its noise, giving more signal and less noise. Better sensitivity = cleaner recovered signal.
16-5: Selectivity is the ability to separate signals that are close in frequency, rejecting the unwanted neighbour. Selective = picks one of two close signals.
16-6: High selectivity comes from a narrow bandwidth, which passes the wanted signal while excluding adjacent ones. Narrow bandwidth means high selectivity.
16-7: The BFO beats against the IF signal to make an audible tone, so it operates very close to the IF frequency. BFO sits near the IF.
16-8: For Morse the BFO beats with the IF signal to create an audible tone, since keyed CW itself carries no audio. The beat turns silent CW into a heard note.
16-9: SSB has its carrier suppressed, so a product detector reinserts a carrier to recover the audio. Product detectors suit suppressed-carrier SSB.
16-10: SSB transmits with the carrier removed, so the receiver's insertion oscillator supplies a replacement carrier for detection. It puts back the missing carrier.
16-11: The RF amplifier has both input and output tuned to the received frequency, since it operates before any frequency conversion. It works right at the signal frequency.
16-12: Adding an RF amplifier before the mixer boosts weak signals above the mixer's noise, increasing overall sensitivity. Front-end gain improves sensitivity.
16-13: Different modes need different bandwidths, so selectable IF filters let the operator match the passband to the signal being received. Pick a filter to fit the mode's bandwidth.
16-14: The mixer takes a tuneable input signal and outputs a fixed IF, so it has a tuneable input and fixed-tuned output. Mixer converts variable RF to a set IF.
16-15: The mixer combines the signal with the local oscillator to produce the fixed intermediate frequency used by later stages. Mixing creates the IF.
16-16: A mixer produces the sum and difference of its inputs: 16 minus 7 gives 9 MHz and 16 plus 7 gives 23 MHz. Mixer outputs are sum and difference frequencies.
16-17: A baseband SDR must sample above twice the highest frequency (Nyquist), so 150 MHz supports up to about 75 MHz, reaching the 6m (50 MHz) band but not 2m. Sample rate limits the top usable band.
16-18: AGC means automatic gain control, which automatically adjusts receiver gain to keep output steady despite fading signal strength. AGC evens out volume automatically.
16-19: A direct-conversion SDR uses in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) signals 90 degrees apart to capture full signal information and resolve sidebands. Quadrature means a 90 degree offset.
16-20: Tuning changes the local oscillator frequency, which shifts which incoming signal converts down to the fixed IF. You tune the LO, not the IF.
16-21: The LO must differ from the 14 MHz signal by the 500 kHz IF, so 14 MHz plus 0.5 MHz gives 14.5 MHz. LO equals signal plus (or minus) the IF.
16-22: The audio leaving the detector is too weak to drive a speaker, so an audio amplifier is needed to raise it. Detector output is faint and needs boosting.
16-23: An output transformer matches the amplifier's output impedance to the low-impedance loudspeaker for efficient power transfer. It matches impedances for maximum transfer.
16-24: A single-conversion SSB superhet has the local oscillator plus the carrier insertion oscillator, making two oscillators. LO plus reinserted carrier equals two.
16-25: A signal spaced from the wanted one by twice the IF (here 1 MHz, twice 500 kHz) is the image frequency that mixes to the same IF. Images sit two IFs away.
16-26: The IF equals the difference between LO and signal: 3995 minus 3540 kHz gives 455 kHz. IF is the LO-to-signal difference.
16-27: Double conversion uses two mixers, each needing its own local oscillator and IF stage, giving two IF stages and two local oscillators. Each conversion adds an oscillator and IF.
16-28: Converting first to a high IF then a low one pushes the image frequency far away, so double conversion gives better image rejection. Two conversions improve image rejection.
16-29: A squelch circuit mutes the speaker when no signal is present, silencing background noise until a signal appears. Squelch quiets the hiss between transmissions.
17-0: A crystal oscillator provides a very stable, precise reference frequency because the quartz crystal resonates at a fixed rate. Crystal equals rock-solid frequency stability.
17-1: A balanced modulator cancels the carrier while producing both sidebands, giving double sideband suppressed carrier, the first step in generating SSB. Balanced means the carrier is cancelled out.
17-2: After DSB suppressed carrier, a sharp filter removes one sideband to leave single sideband, saving bandwidth and power. The filter keeps just one sideband.
17-3: The mixer heterodynes the generated SSB signal up to the desired operating frequency. In a transmitter the mixer translates the signal to the wanted band.
17-4: SSB carries amplitude information, so it needs a linear amplifier that boosts the signal without distortion to avoid splatter. Linear preserves the SSB waveform faithfully.
17-5: VFO means variable frequency oscillator, letting the operator tune the transmit frequency continuously across a band. VFO = tuneable frequency source.
17-6: The master oscillator generates a steady, continuous signal at the wanted carrier frequency, setting the transmitted frequency. Master oscillator = stable carrier source.
17-7: A driver/buffer isolates the oscillator from the power amplifier so PA loading changes cannot pull the oscillator off frequency. Buffer shields the oscillator from the PA.
17-8: In this keyed transmitter the Morse key gates the oscillator signal, passing RF only while the key is pressed to form dots and dashes. Key down lets the signal through.
17-9: The power amplifier raises the low-level RF to the output power needed to drive the antenna. PA = final power boost before the antenna.
17-10: The speech amplifier boosts the weak microphone audio to a usable level for the modulator. It simply amplifies the mic signal.
17-11: In an FM transmitter the modulator uses the speech waveform to shift (vary) the oscillator frequency, which is how FM is produced. Voice bends the frequency for FM.
17-12: The FM transmitter's oscillator is a variable-frequency RF oscillator whose frequency is shifted by the modulation. It runs at RF and is tuneable.
17-13: A frequency multiplier outputs a harmonic (integer multiple) of the oscillator, raising both the frequency and, usefully, the FM deviation. Multiplier makes a harmonic of the input.
17-14: The power amplifier boosts the RF signal to the level required to drive the antenna. PA delivers the final RF power.
17-15: Full AM produces a carrier plus an upper and a lower sideband. AM = carrier plus two sidebands.
17-16: In FM the carrier's frequency varies in step with the modulating waveform while amplitude stays constant. FM changes frequency, not amplitude.
17-17: A balanced modulator cancels the carrier but leaves both sidebands, giving double sideband suppressed carrier. Balanced kills the carrier, keeps two sidebands.
17-18: CW (Morse) is simply an unmodulated RF carrier switched on and off to form the dots and dashes of characters. CW is keyed RF, on for a mark.
17-19: FM has constant amplitude, so a non-linear (more efficient) amplifier can boost it without distorting the information. Constant amplitude tolerates non-linear amplification.
18-0: Morse (CW) keys the carrier on and off, so the RF is simply switched between full output and nothing. Think of the key as a switch interrupting a steady carrier.
18-1: A VFO's frequency drifts if its supply voltage varies, so a well-regulated, ripple-free DC supply keeps the oscillator's operating point steady and the frequency stable.
18-2: SSB sends only one sideband and suppresses the carrier and the other sideband, so it needs roughly half the bandwidth of double-sideband AM while concentrating all power in the wanted signal.
18-3: A balanced modulator cancels the carrier through symmetry, leaving both sidebands; a filter then removes one to make SSB. Remember: 'balanced' means the carrier balances out to zero.
18-4: FM carries voice as frequency shift (deviation); too much deviation over-swings the signal beyond the receiver's passband, causing distortion. Keep deviation within the channel limits.
18-5: The driver amplifies the low-level signal just enough to properly drive the power amplifier that follows it. Signal chain: oscillator, buffer, driver, then final PA.
18-6: The final (power) amplifier boosts the signal to the level needed for transmission, delivering maximum power to the antenna without changing the frequency.
18-7: No amplifier is 100% efficient, so the DC power that isn't converted to RF output becomes waste heat in the transistors or valve, which is why finals need heatsinking.
18-8: Modulation impresses information (voice, data, Morse) onto a radio carrier so it can be carried over the air; demodulation later recovers it at the receiver.
18-9: Because an SSB signal's amplitude varies with speech, its power is rated by peak envelope power (PEP), the average power at the crest of the largest modulation peak.
19-0: Harmonics fall at whole-number multiples of the fundamental; twice 3525 kHz is 7050 kHz, the second harmonic. Just multiply the base frequency by 2, 3, 4 and so on.
19-1: The third harmonic is three times the fundamental: 3 x 7 MHz = 21 MHz. Harmonic number simply multiplies the base frequency.
19-2: The fifth harmonic is five times the fundamental: 5 x 7 MHz = 35 MHz.
19-3: Driving an amplifier too hard pushes it into clipping and nonlinearity, which distorts the sine wave and generates strong harmonics. Overdrive equals distortion equals harmonics.
19-4: Over-modulating an RF amplifier drives it into nonlinear operation, distorting the waveform and generating harmonics. Keep modulation within limits to stay clean.
19-5: A tuned (resonant) circuit between stages passes the wanted fundamental and rejects the harmonic multiples, filtering them out before the signal reaches the antenna.
19-6: A pure sine wave has only its fundamental; any distortion of its shape adds harmonic content. Distortion and harmonics are two views of the same thing.
19-7: By definition harmonics occur at integer multiples (2x, 3x, 4x...) of the fundamental frequency, always above it, never below.
19-8: 10 metres is around 28-29 MHz; doubling that gives roughly 57 MHz, so 57 MHz is the second harmonic of a 10 metre signal.
19-9: A wave trap is a tuned circuit that resonates at one specific harmonic and shunts or blocks it, targeting a single troublesome frequency in the output.
19-10: A low-pass filter passes the wanted lower fundamental but attenuates the higher harmonic frequencies, reducing harmonic radiation from HF transmitters.
19-11: A low-pass filter passes the fundamental and rejects the higher harmonics; fitting it right at the transmitter output stops harmonics before they reach the feedline or antenna.
19-12: A low-pass filter attenuates frequencies above its cutoff, so it reduces the harmonics that lie above the wanted fundamental.
19-13: A spurious emission is any unwanted output not harmonically related to the wanted signal, such as mixer products or parasitics; harmonics are counted separately.
19-14: A parasitic oscillation is an unwanted self-oscillation that arises within a transmitter, usually in an amplifier stage, unrelated to the intended signal.
19-15: Small chokes, ferrite beads or resistors add loss at the parasitic frequency, damping the stray resonances that let an amplifier self-oscillate.
19-16: Stray lead inductance and capacitance can form resonances both above and below the operating frequency, so parasitics may appear at either high or low frequencies.
19-17: Parasitic oscillations arise from accidental stray resonances in the circuit, so they appear at frequencies unrelated to the transmitter's intended output.
19-18: High-gain stages have plenty of amplification to sustain any accidental feedback, making them the most prone to breaking into unwanted parasitic oscillation.
19-19: Because parasitics come from stray circuit resonances rather than the signal itself, their frequency bears no fixed relationship to the operating frequency.
20-0: A mains DC power supply converts the AC mains into a steady DC voltage at a level suitable for running electronic equipment, through transforming, rectifying and smoothing.
20-1: Rectification converts AC to DC; a full-wave diode bridge uses four diodes to flip both halves of the AC cycle into one-directional current.
20-2: After rectification the DC still pulses, so a large electrolytic capacitor stores charge and fills the gaps, smoothing the ripple into steadier DC.
20-3: A 25 W VHF set needs a 12 V source able to supply several amps; a car battery delivers that easily, whereas small plug-packs or low-voltage cells cannot.
20-4: Full-wave rectification produces two output pulses per mains cycle, so with NZ's 50 Hz mains the ripple appears at 2 x 50 = 100 Hz.
20-5: Smoothing needs to store lots of charge, requiring a large capacitance; 10,000 uF is in the right range, while pico- and nanofarad values are far too small.
20-6: A fuse in the mains lead disconnects the supply if a fault draws excessive current, preventing fire or damage. Always fuse on the live mains side.
20-7: Half-wave rectification passes only one half of each AC cycle, giving one pulse per cycle, so with 50 Hz mains the ripple frequency stays at 50 Hz.
20-8: Every supply has some internal resistance, so drawing current produces a voltage drop inside it, making the output sag as the load increases.
20-9: Electrolytics pack large capacitance into a small, low-cost package with low internal resistance, ideal for the bulk energy storage needed to smooth a supply.
21-0: The filter (usually a large capacitor) smooths the pulsating output of the rectifier into steadier DC by storing charge and filling the ripple valleys.
21-1: The regulator holds the output voltage constant despite changes in load current or input voltage, so equipment sees a steady, stable supply.
21-2: The transformer steps the mains AC up or down to a more convenient AC voltage for the rectifier, while also isolating equipment from the mains.
21-3: The rectifier converts the transformer's AC into pulsating (fluctuating) DC that flows in one direction only; smoothing comes later in the filter.
21-4: A three-terminal regulator chip (input, output, ground) is a common, compact way to hold the output voltage constant in a low-power supply.
21-5: A reverse diode across a regulator protects it: if the output ever rises above the input (e.g. a charged load), the diode bypasses the reverse voltage safely around the chip.
21-6: A crowbar across the output shorts the supply the instant voltage exceeds a safe level, blowing the fuse and protecting the connected transceiver from over-voltage damage.
21-7: The crowbar is last-ditch protection: if the regulator fails and lets the voltage rise, it short-circuits the output to blow the fuse before equipment is destroyed.
21-8: Current limiting caps the maximum output current, protecting the regulator's pass transistor from overheating and damage if the output is short-circuited.
21-9: The series pass transistor carries the heavy load current under the regulator's control, letting the supply deliver far more current than a small regulator chip could alone.
22-0: The convention is to say the other station's callsign first, then your own, so listeners immediately know who is being called and who is speaking.
22-1: The ITU standard phonetic alphabet renders ZL1AN as zulu lima one alpha november, ensuring each letter is unmistakable over a noisy channel.
22-2: Standard SSB practice is to send CQ a few times then identify with your callsign a few times, so a listener can catch both the call and who is making it.
22-3: RS reports give readability first (1-5) then strength (1-9); '5 and 1' means perfectly readable but a very weak signal. Readability then strength.
22-4: Using the ITU phonetic alphabet, VK5ZX is victor kilo five zulu xray. Note 'kilo', not 'kilowatt'.
22-5: To announce you are monitoring a repeater, simply give your callsign and state you are listening on it, keeping it brief and clear.
22-6: On CW, 'up 2' means the DX station is working split and listening 2 kHz above its transmit frequency, so callers move up to avoid a pileup on his frequency.
22-7: Pausing about 3 seconds between overs lets the repeater reset, drops any timeout, and allows other stations or emergency traffic to break in.
22-8: Always listen first and then ask if the frequency is in use, so you avoid transmitting on top of a contact you cannot yet hear.
22-9: 'Fully quieting' means your signal into the repeater is strong enough to completely silence the receiver's background noise, giving clean, noise-free output.
23-0: 'Dropping out' means your signal into the repeater is too weak to reliably hold it open, so the repeater keeps losing you and cutting off your audio.
23-1: A pileup is the crowd of stations all transmitting at once to work a single rare DX station, creating a wall of competing callers.
23-2: Break-in (QSK) keying lets a CW operator hear the band in the gaps between his own Morse elements, so he can detect a station breaking in mid-transmission.
23-3: A positive split means the repeater listens (receives) 600 kHz above the frequency you tune to, while transmitting on the designated frequency. You transmit high, it outputs low.
23-4: NZ 2 metre repeaters use a 600 kHz offset: positive above 147 MHz and negative on or below 147 MHz, telling your radio which way to shift for transmit.
23-5: NZ 70 cm (UHF) repeaters use a standard offset of plus or minus 5 MHz between input and output frequencies.
23-6: An SWR bridge shows reflected power from a mismatch; adjusting the matching unit for minimum reflected power means maximum power is transferred to the antenna.
23-7: Squelch mutes the audio during no signal, silencing background hiss, and only opens to let you hear when an incoming signal is present.
23-8: The S meter shows relative received signal strength, letting you compare how strong different incoming signals are.
23-9: The National System is a network of linked amateur repeaters in the 70 cm band, allowing wide-area communication across New Zealand.
23-10: A noise blanker works best on sharp, impulsive noise like vehicle ignition sparks, gating out the brief spikes between signal peaks.
23-11: VOX switches the transceiver from receive to transmit automatically when it detects the operator's voice, giving hands-free operation without the PTT.
23-12: VOX stands for Voice Operated Transmit, meaning the sound of your voice keys the transmitter.
23-13: RIT stands for Receiver Incremental Tuning, a control for fine-tuning the receiver.
23-14: RIT shifts the receive frequency slightly without moving the transmit frequency, so you can tune in a slightly off-frequency station while still answering on the original frequency.
23-15: Split frequency operation lets you transmit on one frequency and receive on another, essential for working DX stations that listen away from their transmit frequency.
23-16: ALC stands for Automatic Level Control, which limits transmitter drive to prevent overdriving and distortion.
23-17: AGC automatically adjusts receiver gain to keep loud and weak signals at similar audio levels, so you needn't constantly ride the gain control.
23-18: Separate RF and AF gain controls let you set the radio-frequency amplifier gain and the audio amplifier gain independently for best signal handling and comfortable volume.
23-19: PTT means Push To Talk: pressing the button switches the transceiver from receive to transmit while you speak.
24-0: QRM refers to man-made interference from other transmissions. Distinguish it from QRN, which is natural static (N for Nature/Noise). Think 'M for Man-made' interference on your signal.
24-1: QRN means troubled by static, i.e. natural atmospheric noise like lightning crashes. Remember 'N for Noise/Nature', versus QRM which is man-made interference.
24-2: QRS asks the other station to send more slowly. Handy hook: 'S for Slow'. Its opposite, QRQ, means send faster.
24-3: QRZ? asks 'who is calling me?'. It is commonly heard after a busy call when an operator wants the callers to identify themselves again.
24-4: QTH means location or position. The QT- signals relate to traffic and place; QTH is the standard shorthand for 'my location is'.
24-5: QRL? asks whether a frequency or station is busy, typically sent before transmitting to check a frequency is clear. 'Is this frequency in use?'
24-6: QRP relates to transmitter power; QRP? asks 'shall I decrease power?'. Amateurs use 'QRP' to describe low-power operating.
24-7: QSB indicates signal fading, the slow rise and fall of strength caused by changing propagation. Hook: 'B for Bouncing/varying' signal strength.
24-8: QSY means change frequency; QSY? asks 'shall I change to another frequency?'. Operators say 'let's QSY' when moving off a busy channel.
24-9: QRQ means send faster ('Q for Quick'), the opposite of QRS (send Slower). Both are Morse speed requests.
25-0: When a line is terminated in its characteristic impedance, the load absorbs all the energy with no reflections, so the source cannot tell the line is finite. It behaves like an infinitely long line.
25-1: Characteristic impedance depends only on the geometry: conductor diameter, spacing, and the dielectric between them. It is independent of length or frequency.
25-2: Characteristic impedance is set by the cable's construction, not its length. Cutting a 52-ohm line to any length leaves it 52 ohms.
25-3: A quarter-wave ground plane has a feed impedance near 50 ohms and is an unbalanced antenna, so unbalanced 50-ohm coax matches it well.
25-4: Modern transmitters are designed for a nominal 50-ohm output, the industry standard that matches common coax and antennas for efficient power transfer.
25-5: Maximum power transfer occurs when source and load impedances match. A correct match between transmitter and antenna ensures energy is delivered rather than reflected.
25-6: Coaxial cable has a central conductor surrounded by insulating dielectric, then an outer braid shield, all sharing one axis ('co-axial'). The braid confines and shields the RF field.
25-7: Matching the line at the transmitter end presents the correct load to the amplifier so it delivers maximum power to the antenna rather than reflecting it back.
25-8: An incorrect load causes reflected power and high standing waves, so the output stage cannot deliver energy properly and dissipates it as excessive heat, risking damage.
25-9: When the amplifier and antenna are mismatched, some power is reflected instead of radiated, so less energy leaves the antenna and radiation is reduced.
25-10: Feedline losses convert some RF into heat in the cable, so less power reaches the antenna and is radiated. Longer or lossier lines waste more power.
25-11: A mismatch between line and antenna causes reflected waves that combine with forward waves to form standing waves on the feedline, raising the SWR.
25-12: Standing waves signify reflected power returning toward the transmitter instead of being radiated, so less RF energy actually reaches and leaves the antenna.
25-13: A shorted quarter-wave line transforms the short (zero ohms) into an open circuit at the input, showing very high (theoretically infinite) impedance. Quarter-wave lines invert impedances.
25-14: A transmit/receive switch must disable the unit not in use, protecting the sensitive receiver from the transmitter's power and preventing both from loading the antenna at once.
25-15: An SWR meter compares forward and reflected power, indicating how well power is transferred to the antenna. A low SWR (near 1:1) means most power is being radiated.
25-16: Open-wire feeder has air as its dielectric and widely spaced conductors, giving very low loss compared with coax, whose solid dielectric adds losses.
25-17: Solid polythene dielectric slows the wave to about 0.66 of the speed in free space, so signals travel at roughly two-thirds speed. This matters when cutting cable to electrical lengths.
25-18: Coaxial cable is self-shielding with its outer braid and jacketed, so surrounding earth does not affect it; it can be buried directly. Open and twinlead types would detune near ground.
25-19: Coax's outer braid shields the inner conductor, so nearby grounded metal does not disturb it. Balanced open-wire or twinlead would be unbalanced by adjacent metal objects.
26-0: The boom is the central supporting spine of a Yagi that carries the elements at right angles; it is structural and does not radiate. In the diagram U marks this long central member.
26-1: The reflector is the longest element, placed behind the driven element, and it reflects energy forward. In the diagram V marks this rear element.
26-2: A director is shorter than the driven element and sits in front, focusing radiation forward. Item X marks the forward parasitic element.
26-3: A resonant half-wave dipole is cut a few percent shorter than a free-space half wavelength because end effects and wire thickness lower its resonant frequency. So X+X is slightly under half a wavelength.
26-4: Parallel-tuned traps act as high impedance at their resonant band, electrically disconnecting the outer sections, so the dipole becomes the right length on several bands.
26-5: Adding a series (loading) inductor adds electrical length, so a physically shorter antenna can remain resonant. This is how mobile whips are kept short.
26-6: Wavelength = 300 / f(MHz). At 1 MHz that is 300 m, so a half wave is 150 m. Practical antennas are trimmed a little shorter.
26-7: Wavelength = 300 / frequency in MHz, so 300 / 25 = 12 metres. This formula converts any frequency to wavelength.
26-8: An electromagnetic wave has its electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other, and both perpendicular to the direction of travel. This orthogonal relationship is fundamental.
26-9: Polarisation is defined by the orientation of the electric field. A vertical electric field means a vertically polarised wave; a horizontal one means horizontal polarisation.
26-10: At the centre of a half-wave dipole current is maximum and voltage minimum, giving a low feed impedance (near 73 ohms) that is easy to match. Feed it at the current maximum.
