26-11: Antenna height above ground sets the radiation angle. A low horizontal antenna radiates at high angles (good for local/NVIS), while a higher one lowers the angle for DX.
26-12: A vertical over a ground plane is omnidirectional in the horizontal plane, radiating equally to all compass points, unlike a dipole which has a figure-eight pattern.
26-13: A ground plane's vertical radiating element produces a vertical electric field, so it emits a vertically polarised wave. Vertical element means vertical polarisation.
26-14: A folded dipole steps the impedance up about four times that of a plain dipole (roughly 73 ohms), giving near 300 ohms, which suits 300-ohm ribbon feeder.
26-15: A half-wave dipole in free space has a centre feed impedance of about 73 ohms, which is why 75-ohm coax is a reasonable match. Height above ground shifts this value.
26-16: Series inductance adds electrical length (loading), which lowers the resonant frequency. Inductors lengthen electrically; capacitors shorten.
26-17: A balun connects a balanced load (like a dipole) to an unbalanced line (coax), matching the two so current stays balanced. 'Balun' = BALanced-to-UNbalanced.
26-18: A dummy antenna (dummy load) is a resistive load matching the antenna's impedance, letting a transmitter be tested and tuned without radiating a signal on air.
26-19: A half wave equals 150 / f(MHz) approximately for real wire; at 7.1 MHz that is about 20 metres. This is the 40-metre band dipole length.
26-20: A dipole with 20 m each side totals 40 m, which is a half wavelength of about 80 m, corresponding to roughly 3600 kHz. Use f = 150 / half-length.
26-21: A dipole also resonates at odd harmonics. A 7 MHz antenna works at 21 MHz (its third harmonic), which is the 15-metre band.
26-22: Bandwidth is the span of frequencies over which an antenna works acceptably (low SWR). Wider bandwidth means usable over a larger frequency range without retuning.
26-23: Shortening the radiating element raises the resonant frequency, since a shorter antenna resonates at a higher frequency. Shorter = higher, longer = lower.
26-24: End insulators stop the antenna current at a defined point, fixing the wire's electrical length and isolating it from supports so its resonance is controlled.
26-25: Lengthening the antenna lowers its resonant frequency, because a longer element resonates lower. To go lower in frequency, add wire.
26-26: A half-wave antenna fed at the centre has two poles (legs), hence 'dipole'. It is the fundamental reference antenna.
26-27: A dipole's resonant frequency is set mainly by its physical length; longer resonates lower, shorter higher. Feedline length and power do not change resonance.
26-28: A quarter-wave vertical uses the car body as its ground plane, is compact at 28 MHz, and radiates omnidirectionally, making it ideal for mobile mounting.
26-29: A quarter-wave ground plane uses a conductive surface (radials or a metal sheet) at its base to act as the missing half of the antenna, mirroring the vertical element.
26-30: A vertical antenna is omnidirectional, receiving and transmitting equally from all horizontal directions, unlike directional beams. Good for not knowing where signals come from.
26-31: At the ends of a dipole the current falls to zero while voltage peaks, giving high voltage and low current. The centre is the opposite: high current, low voltage.
26-32: A delta loop is a full-wavelength triangular loop practical to build at HF, whereas parabolic dishes and multi-element Yagis are more suited to VHF/UHF where wavelengths are short.
26-33: A Yagi has gain because its parasitic elements concentrate radiation into one direction rather than radiating everywhere; it focuses the same power, not creates more.
26-34: A Yagi radiates toward the director end of the boom (away from the reflector). The signal fires forward past the shorter directors.
26-35: The reflector and directors are not directly fed; they are excited by the driven element's field, so they are called parasitic elements.
26-36: An isotropic antenna is a theoretical point source radiating equally in all directions in three dimensions. It cannot be built but serves as a gain reference (dBi).
26-37: A 5/8-wave vertical concentrates radiation at a low angle to the horizon, giving better range for VHF mobile and base work than a simpler quarter-wave.
26-38: For long-distance (DX) work the radiation angle matters most: a low takeoff angle lets signals reach the ionosphere at a shallow angle and skip further.
26-39: On HF the ionosphere twists and randomises a signal's polarisation as it refracts, so matching transmit and receive antenna polarisation matters little, unlike line-of-sight VHF/UHF.
27-0: The skip zone is the dead area between where the ground wave fades out and where the first sky wave (refracted off the ionosphere) returns to earth. Neither wave reaches this gap, so signals cannot be heard there.
27-1: The ionosphere is the layer of ionised gas that refracts HF waves back to earth, enabling long-distance skip. Remember 'iono' for ions, the charged particles that bend the signal.
27-2: MUF (Maximum Usable Frequency) is the highest frequency the ionosphere will still bend back to earth for a given path; above it, signals punch through into space. Higher ionisation raises the MUF.
27-3: The sun drives ionisation and disturbances across the whole spectrum, so all communications frequencies are ultimately governed by solar activity. The sun is the master switch for radio propagation.
27-4: The sunspot (solar) cycle averages about 11 years from peak to peak, alternating between high and low ionisation that greatly affects HF band openings. Think '11 years' for the rhythm of the sun.
27-5: The skywave is the ionospheric wave: energy radiated upward that is refracted by the ionosphere back to earth, giving long-distance HF contacts. Sky wave equals bounce off the ionosphere.
27-6: Polarisation is defined by the orientation of the electric (E) field. A vertical E field means vertical polarisation, which is why antenna orientation must match for best reception.
27-7: The ground wave is the portion of HF energy that travels along and is guided by the earth's surface, dominating short-range coverage before the wave leaves the ground.
27-8: The low D layer absorbs rather than reflects, and during daylight it heavily absorbs frequencies below about 4 MHz. The D layer disappears at night, which is why the lower bands come alive after dark.
27-9: The E layer sits above the absorbing D layer; high-angle low-frequency waves that slip through the D layer are refracted back by the E layer during the day.
27-10: Sporadic-E is patchy, intense ionisation forming seasonally at E-layer height, allowing surprise openings on VHF and the higher HF bands. 'Sporadic' captures its unpredictable, seasonal nature.
27-11: A low radiation angle (under about 30 degrees) launches the wave at a shallow angle so it travels far before returning to earth, maximising hop distance. Low angle equals long distance.
27-12: At VHF and above, the ionosphere no longer bends signals, so they travel in essentially straight lines like light, limiting range to roughly line-of-sight.
27-13: When a signal arrives via multiple paths of differing length, the waves drift in and out of phase, alternately reinforcing and cancelling to cause fading (multipath fading).
27-14: The skip zone is the silent gap between the end of the ground wave and the point where the first sky wave lands, where neither wave provides coverage.
27-15: HF long-distance work relies on ionospheric reflection (refraction), bending waves back to earth so they hop far beyond the horizon. Without the ionosphere, HF DX would not happen.
27-16: The high F layer is the main long-haul reflector: being the highest layer it allows the longest hops, and it persists at night, making it the workhorse for DX.
27-17: Ionisation is lowest just before sunrise, after a full night with no solar input to replenish the charged particles. The ionosphere is most depleted at dawn's first light.
27-18: Solar radiation splits the F layer into F1 and F2 during the day; they recombine into a single F layer at night. Remember F for the layer that forks in daylight.
27-19: Sudden ionospheric disturbances and storms stem from solar flares, which blast the ionosphere with radiation and particles, disrupting or fading HF propagation.
27-20: 80 metres works well at night for regional contacts up to a few thousand kilometres, but suffers high atmospheric and man-made noise. Daytime D-layer absorption limits it to short range.
27-21: Skip distance depends on both the ionosphere's height and the antenna's radiation angle: a higher layer or shallower angle both push the first return point further away.
27-22: The three propagation-affecting ionospheric layers are D, E and F. Remember them in order of increasing altitude: D absorbs, E and F reflect.
27-23: In summer daylight the D layer is strongly ionised and absorbs 80 metre energy, so signals are soaked up before they can hop far, limiting range to short distances.
27-24: Skip distance is measured from the transmitter to the nearest point where the sky wave first returns to earth, unlike the skip zone which is the gap between ground and sky wave.
27-25: Fading is the slow rise and fall in signal strength caused by changing path lengths making multipath signals drift in and out of phase at the receiver.
27-26: VHF/UHF satellite links work because these frequencies pass through the ionosphere with little bending or absorption, so signals reach the satellite in space instead of being reflected back.
27-27: The critical frequency is the highest frequency reflected straight back when sent vertically; above it, signals sent straight up escape into space. It sets the baseline for the MUF at other angles.
27-28: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves and travel at the speed of light (about 300,000 km/s in free space), just like visible light.
27-29: MUF simply stands for Maximum Usable Frequency, the top frequency the ionosphere will still return to earth on a given path at a given time.
27-30: The E layer lies below the F layer and above the D layer, following the D-E-F order of increasing height in the ionosphere.
27-31: Selective fading affects different sidebands of an AM signal unequally, distorting the modulation on distant sky-wave signals while a local ground-wave station stays clean.
27-32: Skip effects arise from reflection and refraction of the wave by the ionosphere, which bends the signal back to earth some distance from the transmitter.
27-33: Ionised layers, where solar radiation strips electrons from gas atoms, are what refract radio signals back to earth. Charged particles, not clouds, do the reflecting.
27-34: The ionosphere consists of layers of ionised gases surrounding the earth, created when solar radiation knocks electrons free from atmospheric atoms at high altitude.
27-35: Skip distance is greatest with the smallest radiation angle, because a shallow launch angle sends the wave far downrange before it returns to earth. Low angle equals long skip.
27-36: Raising the reflecting layer's height increases skip distance, since a higher bounce point geometrically pushes the return point further away from the transmitter.
27-37: When the frequency exceeds the Maximum Usable Frequency, the ionosphere can no longer bend it back and the signal passes through into space instead of returning.
27-38: Line-of-sight transmission between nearby stations relies mainly on the ground wave (direct/surface wave), not on ionospheric reflection.
27-39: Ground wave range shrinks as frequency rises, because higher frequencies are absorbed more quickly by the earth. Lower bands like 160 m give the best ground-wave coverage.
27-40: The wave that goes up to the ionosphere and is refracted back to earth is the sky wave, the mechanism behind long-distance HF communication.
27-41: HF signals travelling beyond about 4000 km arrive via the sky wave, hopping off the ionosphere, since the ground wave dies out over far shorter distances.
27-42: 28 MHz (10 metres) needs strong daytime ionisation to reach the high MUF that supports it, so it opens for DX during daylight, especially near solar maximum.
27-43: How many HF bands are open depends on the highest frequency the ionosphere can still reflect (the MUF): the higher the MUF, the more bands are usable for DX.
27-44: The ionosphere follows the roughly 11-year sunspot cycle, with ionisation and band conditions rising and falling over that period. Remember 11 years for the solar rhythm.
27-45: Because the ionosphere constantly shifts, small changes alter the path and produce variations in received signal strength, the everyday cause of fading on HF.
27-46: Ionospheric storms disrupt the layers and typically cause sky-wave signals to fade out, since the disturbed ionosphere can no longer reliably reflect HF.
27-47: Fading is the term for the changes in received strength that occur with sky-wave propagation as the ionosphere and path lengths vary.
27-48: The ionosphere changes continuously with time of day and solar conditions, so a path open now may close within an hour as the MUF or layer heights shift.
27-49: VHF/UHF signals reflect easily off buildings and other solid objects, so energy can bounce and arrive at a receiver off the direct path, sometimes from an unexpected direction.
28-0: EMC is about equipment coexisting: working properly in its environment while not emitting disturbances that upset other equipment. Think 'good electromagnetic neighbour' — it functions and doesn't cause trouble.
28-1: An audible hum usually means residual mains ripple (50 Hz) is riding on the DC supply and modulating the RF. A properly rated, well-regulated and filtered DC supply removes that ripple.
28-2: Harmonics are exact multiples of the transmit frequency, so they appear as discrete narrow-band signals. Broadband noise sources like sparks or motors instead smear energy across many frequencies.
28-3: A commutator with worn brushes sparks continuously as it switches, radiating impulse noise spread across a wide frequency range. Sparking equals broadband continuous interference.
28-4: Overhead power lines arc across dirty or cracked insulators, and rain changes the leakage and arcing, so the noise level shifts with weather. Rain-dependent buzz points to the lines outside.
28-5: First rule out your own gear: if your own domestic equipment is clean, you've demonstrated the problem is the neighbour's poorly-immune device, not your transmitter. Check your own house first.
28-6: Overdriving the audio (speech) stages creates distortion and harmonics that widen the transmitted bandwidth, producing splatter onto adjacent frequencies. Too much audio equals a signal that's too wide.
28-7: Using only the minimum power needed to maintain contact reduces field strength at neighbours' equipment and the chance of interference. Low power, fewer complaints — good practice everywhere.
28-8: Correlating complaints with your logged transmission times objectively confirms whether you are the source before assigning blame. The log is your evidence.
28-9: Cross-modulation happens when a strong signal is rectified by a non-linear junction (a diode-like semiconductor or corroded joint), transferring one signal's modulation onto another. Non-linearity plus strong signal equals cross-mod.
28-10: Audio-stage overload means the RF is detected after the tuning circuits, so the receiver's dial setting is irrelevant — the interference appears at every tuning position. Heard everywhere means front-end/audio overload.
28-11: Cross-modulation transfers the unwanted transmission onto the wanted signal, so the interfering audio is heard mixed into the desired station's programme. It rides in the background of what you want to hear.
28-12: Any transmitter emission outside its intended channel — harmonics and other spurious products — can interfere with other users and must be suppressed. Harmonics and spurii are the 'unwanted extras'.
28-13: Harmonics are always higher than the fundamental, so a low-pass filter passes the wanted signal and blocks the higher harmonics; placing it right at the transmitter stops harmonics before they radiate.
28-14: An incorrectly connected or unbalanced feedline lets RF flow back on the outer conductor into the shack, causing feedback and interference. Bad antenna connection sends RF back down the line.
28-15: The filter belongs at the transmitter output so it removes harmonics and spurious emissions before they reach the antenna and radiate. Clean the signal at the source.
28-16: A band-pass filter passes a chosen band and rejects everything on both sides, so it attenuates frequencies on each side of the passband. Keep the middle, cut the edges.
28-17: A band-stop (notch) filter blocks one band and lets everything else through, so frequencies on each side of the stopband pass freely. Opposite of band-pass.
28-18: An HF transmitter's fundamentals are below 30 MHz, so a low-pass filter passes those and attenuates the higher harmonics above 30 MHz. Pass low, block high.
28-19: A low-pass filter blocks frequencies above the cutoff, so harmonics higher than the operating frequency are prevented from reaching the antenna and radiating. High frequencies stopped.
28-20: A low-pass filter passes the wanted lower frequency and attenuates anything higher, such as harmonics above the transmit frequency. Low-pass attenuates the highs.
28-21: Harmonics are higher-frequency multiples, so a low-pass filter at the transmitter output stops them radiating while passing the wanted signal. Put the low-pass right at the transmitter.
28-22: Electric field strength is a voltage gradient over distance, measured in volts per metre. Field strength = volts per metre; magnetic field would be amps per metre.
28-23: Common-mode current flows on the outside of the feedline; a toroid/ferrite choke adds impedance to that outer current without affecting the balanced signal inside. A choke balun kills common-mode current.
28-24: A high-pass filter passes frequencies above its cutoff and attenuates those below, so it blocks low frequencies but not high ones. High-pass = highs get through.
28-25: Op-amp filters use negative feedback to set a controlled, stable gain and defined frequency response; positive feedback would make it oscillate. Op-amp filters rely on negative feedback.
28-26: An op-amp has enormous open-loop gain at low frequencies, which is deliberately tamed by feedback components to a useful, stable value. Huge raw gain, reined in by feedback.
28-27: An ideal op-amp draws almost no input current, meaning very high input impedance so it barely loads the source. High input impedance is a defining op-amp trait.
28-28: An active filter uses an op-amp for gain combined with resistors and capacitors setting the cutoff — no bulky inductors needed. Op-amp plus RC equals active filter.
28-29: A notch filter attenuates a very narrow band centred on one frequency, deeply rejecting that spot while passing the rest. Narrow deep cut equals notch.
29-0: Modem is short for modulator/demodulator: it modulates outgoing data onto a carrier and demodulates incoming signals back to data. The name is literally the two functions combined.
29-1: A modem converts digital data into audio tones for transmitting and turns received audio tones back into digital data. It's the bridge between bits and sound.
29-2: A computer sound-card can generate and sample audio tones, so with software it performs modem duties — turning data into transmit audio and decoding received audio. Sound-card = software modem.
29-3: FT8, RTTY and PSK31 are all genuine digital keyboard/data modes. The other options mix in analogue modes or non-mode abbreviations like AGC and AFC, which are receiver controls.
29-4: FSK is Frequency Shift Keying: data is sent by shifting the carrier between two (or more) frequencies representing mark and space. Shift the frequency to send the bits.
29-5: Binary 11011011 equals 128+64+16+8+2+1 = 219. Convert by summing the place values where a 1 appears.
29-6: Multipath spreads symbols in time, causing inter-symbol errors; sending slower (lower baud) lengthens each symbol so the delayed echoes overlap less. Slow down to beat multipath.
29-7: FT8 includes forward error correction, adding redundant coding so the receiver can reconstruct data despite errors without asking for a resend. FEC fixes errors at the receiving end.
29-8: APRS is the Automatic Packet Reporting System, using packet radio to share position, telemetry and short messages in real time. Remember: Automatic Packet Reporting System.
29-9: On VHF/UHF, APRS packets are sent as audio tones over standard FM voice channels, matching common FM transceivers. APRS rides on FM at VHF/UHF.
